reframing_when: The question inherits premises from authority, convention, or industry norms without examining whether those premises are actually true — stripping them reveals a different problem.
The question is built on analogy to past situations rather than on the elemental truths of the current situation, and the analogy may not hold.
The question accepts existing categories or market definitions as given when those categories are the very thing distorting the solution space.
The question jumps to 'how do we optimize X' without first asking 'is X the right thing to be doing at all' — the forward-only formulation skips the foundational question.
reframing_move: Strip the question to its elemental truths: what do we actually know is true here, independent of what we've been told or assumed? Rebuild the question from those truths — the reframed question often has a different subject than the original.
curation_note: First-principles thinking is a primary reframing tool because it directly attacks inherited premises in questions. The source is explicit: 'systematically question every assumption underlying a problem' and the 'What would you have to believe?' technique both operate on question-level framing.

reframing_when.note: All four activations from explicit source material: assumption stripping, analogy-over-truth, category distortion, and the foundational-question-skip pattern.

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Borrowed premise is the primary target (inherited framing). Scope lock via category acceptance. Proxy optimization via 'is X the right thing'. Option space collapse via stripping artificial constraints.
